rules.statement: Don't ask an HTTP error message to format the `HttpStatusCode` enum instead of `(int)response.StatusCode`.
rules.why: The numeric status is the standard form in an HTTP error message. Codes such as 425 have no enum member, so the enum prints a number anyway, and `HttpRequestException.StatusCode` already carries the enum for code that needs it.
rules.check: Before reporting a numeric status in an exception or log message, confirm the typed status is still available on the exception. If it is, don't report it.

rules.statement: Name an HTTP status code that `HttpStatusCode` has no member for (such as 425 Too Early) with a named constant instead of writing a bare `(HttpStatusCode)425` cast.
rules.why: A bare numeric cast hides what the status means where it is used.
rules.check: Look for `(HttpStatusCode)<number>` casts in production or test code, including `InlineData` attributes.

rules.statement: Don't discard the bool result of a `TryWrite…`/`TryFormat` call. Validate the input range up front and throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a value outside it, so the try call can't fail, and state that in a comment.
rules.why: An ignored failure lets a broken precondition surface later as an unrelated, misleading exception.
rules.check: Look for `TryWriteBytes`, `TryFormat` or similar calls used as statements without checking their result, and for missing range checks before them.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a private method's parameter to be widened from a concrete collection or buffer type (such as `List<T>` or a concrete buffer writer) to an interface when analyzer CA1859 requires the concrete type.
rules.why: CA1859 is an error under the build's analyzers with warnings as errors, so changing the parameter to the interface fails the build.
rules.check: Before reporting, check whether the method is private or internal and its callers pass only the concrete type. If so, CA1859 decides and there's nothing to report.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a private constructor to be replaced with a primary constructor when it's private so that instances can only be made through a verifying static factory such as `Parse` or `Verify`.
rules.why: A primary constructor can't be private, so the conversion would let any code in the assembly build an unverified instance. The primary-constructor convention covers only types a primary constructor can fully express.
rules.check: Before reporting, check whether the constructor is private and the type has a static factory that validates or verifies its input.

rules.statement: In a test project, put each test in a `#region <Member> Tests` block named for the member under test, including live or integration test files.
rules.why: It keeps every test file laid out the same way as its sibling test files.
rules.check: Look for test methods sitting directly in a test class without the `#region <Member> Tests` grouping that the sibling test files use.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a capped response body to be collected in a pooled buffer writer when the resulting `byte[]` is kept or returned to callers. The pooled-rental rule applies only to transient buffers, such as the read chunk.
rules.why: A body that callers keep (for example, one stored in a cache) isn't a transient buffer, so the transient read chunk is the only buffer that needs to come from `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared`.
rules.check: Before reporting a `MemoryStream`/`ToArray` body, check whether the array outlives the call (it is returned, stored or handed to a cache) and whether the read chunk is already rented.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a catch-all exception translation to be narrowed when the interface contract requires implementations to fail only with one exception type.
rules.why: Narrowing the translation would let raw exceptions escape the interface's documented failure contract.
rules.check: Before reporting a catch-all mapping, check the interface's documented failure contract and the tests that pin the mapping.

rules.statement: Don't report a duplicate-fetch race in a single-flight cache of `Lazy` tasks when successful entries are never removed and a failed entry is removed only by value, with `TryRemove(KeyValuePair.Create(key, fetch))`.
rules.why: Removing an entry only by value means a late caller's `GetOrAdd` receives the completed fetch, not a new one, so no second fetch can start.
rules.check: Before reporting, read how the cache removes entries: unconditional removal by key can race, but compare-and-remove by key and value can't.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a `CancellationToken` parameter on a private shared (single-flight) fetch that is bounded by its own timeout.
rules.why: A fetch shared by many callers must be bounded by its own timeout, not by one caller's token, so that one caller's cancellation doesn't cancel the fetch for everyone else.
rules.check: Before reporting a missing token, check whether the method's result is shared across callers and whether it creates its own timeout `CancellationTokenSource`.

rules.statement: When code is deliberately duplicated in more than one class or package, give each copy a comment saying it is copied on purpose and naming the other copies.
rules.why: Without the marker, a fix to one copy (timeouts, failure memory, race handling) can miss the others.
rules.check: Look for logic that duplicates another class's policy or helper without a 'copied on purpose' comment naming the other copy.

rules.statement: Don't ask a component to log a failure it rethrows or returns when a caller further up already logs that failure with its cause.
rules.why: The central logger already records every failure, and the rethrown exception names the cause, so logging it again adds nothing.
rules.check: Before reporting missing logging, trace where the exception goes and check whether that caller logs it.

rules.statement: End an options-validation failure message for a range or duration with the refused value (for example "; it is {value}."), but never echo values that may carry credentials, such as a base address URI.
rules.why: An operator whose host fails to start can see what was configured, while a URI echoed into a start-up exception could copy a credential into it.
rules.check: Look for range-validation messages that leave out the configured value, and for messages that interpolate URIs or connection strings.

rules.statement: Don't ask for the invariant culture in human-facing exception or validation messages that interpolate non-negative integers or `TimeSpan` values with their default format.
rules.why: Invariant formatting is required only for values meant for machines. These values format the same in every culture, and analyzer CA1305 accepts them.
rules.check: Before reporting, check whether the string is meant for machines (protocol, persistence, a key) and whether the interpolated values could format differently by culture.

rules.statement: Use `stackalloc` buffers, and span overloads such as `SHA512.HashData(source, destination)`, for small fixed-size transient byte values instead of allocating heap arrays.
rules.why: Heap arrays that never outlive the call add avoidable allocations on hot paths such as verification.
rules.check: Look for `new byte[N]` with a small constant N, `ToArray()` or allocating hash overloads whose result is used once and dropped.

rules.statement: Don't ask a read-only text helper to take `ReadOnlySpan<char>` instead of `string` when every caller holds a string, the helper must handle null, or it is used as a method group, such as in `Select`.
rules.why: In those cases the span signature saves nothing or can't be used at all.
rules.check: Before reporting, look at the helper's callers and usages: where they come from, whether null is handled, and whether it is passed as a method group.

rules.statement: Name the sizes that a specification defines (such as RFC 9380's L and count) as constants, and derive buffer sizes and slice offsets from them instead of writing bare literals.
rules.why: A later change to one literal could leave the buffer size and the slice offsets out of step.
rules.check: Look for `stackalloc byte[<literal>]` and range slices with literal offsets that stand for values from a specification.

rules.statement: Don't report a call nested in a `with` initializer, a receiver of `with`/`Build`, a lambda body, a string interpolation or an object creation as a nested-call violation. Don't report a plain two-call chain such as `GetRequiredService<T>().Method()` either, since it isn't a call nested in another call's arguments.
rules.why: These are the exemptions the hoisting convention applies, and a chain isn't nesting.
rules.check: Before reporting a nested call, check whether it's in one of the exempt positions or is only a member-access chain. Report calls nested in another call's arguments, such as `Assert.Equal(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(..), ..)`.

rules.statement: Don't report an `IServiceCollection` local named `services`, or a `JsonElement` that is a parsed response's root named `document`.
rules.why: No naming convention forbids these names, and existing code uses them.
rules.check: Before reporting a naming issue, find the written naming rule and look at how sibling code names the same kind of value.

rules.statement: Don't ask for private static helpers in a static class made only of extension blocks to be moved above the first extension block.
rules.why: The member-order rule places statics before instance members, and a static registration class has no instance members for them to precede.
rules.check: Before reporting member order, check whether the class is static and holds only extension blocks and static helpers.

rules.statement: Mark every member that implements an interface with `/// <inheritdoc/>`, and give private constants and properties a short `///` summary that states units and behavior (for example, a byte count, or that an encoding throws on invalid input).
rules.why: Otherwise IntelliSense shows nothing for the member, and readers aren't told what a constant measures or how a helper behaves.
rules.check: Look for interface implementations with no doc comment, and for new private constants or properties with no `<summary>`.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a `### Changed` changelog entry in a pre-release project. Its changelog describes the product as it is, under Added and Security only, but it must still catalog new options and behavior in every package the change touches.
rules.why: A pre-release project doesn't track changes between versions, yet the release notes must still describe every new setting and behavior.
rules.check: Check AGENTS.md for the project's pre-release status before asking for Changed entries, and check that options and behavior added to any touched package appear in the changelog.
